insights.insight: In late 2024, Sudan experienced fewer recorded battles but far higher lethality per clash, culminating in October’s peak of over 3,200 killed despite only 204 battles.
insights.context: Intro and When Fewer Battles Kill More People section; refs [1][2][3].

insights.insight: From 2023 to 2024, total battles fell 24% (2,579 to 1,961), but distinct battle locations rose from 326 to 417 and affected districts from 110 to 113, indicating wider spatial exposure to conflict despite fewer engagements.
insights.context: When Fewer Battles Kill More People; ref [4].

insights.insight: Average fatalities per battle surged through 2024, from 2.73 in Q1 to 9.07 in Q4, the highest in the two‑year series.
insights.context: When Fewer Battles Kill More People; ref [2].

insights.insight: The correlation between battle frequency and fatalities weakened sharply in 2024 versus 2023, signaling outlier‑driven lethality rather than volume-driven deaths.
insights.context: When Fewer Battles Kill More People; ref [1].

insights.insight: Fatalities were highly concentrated: in 2024, the deadliest 1% of battles caused nearly 30% of battle deaths, and the top 10% caused about two‑thirds.
insights.context: When Fewer Battles Kill More People; ref [6].

insights.insight: By late 2024, Sudan faced the world’s largest displacement crisis, with over 9 million displaced and about 25 million needing aid amid an economy contracted by roughly 18%.
insights.context: When Fewer Battles Kill More People; refs [7][8].

insights.insight: Lethality shifted away from Khartoum: by Q4 2024, over 4,200 battle deaths occurred outside Khartoum versus 139 inside, despite only modest increases in the number of clashes outside.
insights.context: When Fewer Battles Kill More People; ref [9].

insights.insight: Khartoum’s political violence events dropped from ~3,190 in 2023 to ~2,370 in 2024, while Al Jazirah and North Darfur surged to 1,186 and 963 events respectively, becoming new epicenters.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; ref [10].

insights.insight: Outside the capital, Q4 2024 saw soaring fatalities paired with only moderate growth in battles; districts and locations with battles increased nationally, reinforcing dispersion.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; refs [4][9][11].

insights.insight: Ultra‑lethal hubs emerged: in October, ~19 battles in Al Jazirah produced 956 deaths; in December, 56 battles in North Darfur caused 976 deaths.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; ref [12].

insights.insight: At district level, Sharg Al Jazirah averaged over 60 deaths per battle (15 clashes in 2024), Melit about 21, and Al Fasher nearly 10 across 317 battles—extreme outliers in lethality.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; ref [13].

insights.insight: In Q4 2024, Al Fasher and Sharg Al Jazirah together accounted for just over half of all battle deaths; Sharg Al Jazirah logged 903 deaths in 11 events (80+ per clash) and Al Fasher 1,321 deaths in 92 events.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; ref [14].

insights.insight: Excluding districts with average fatalities per battle above 40 strengthened the battle–fatality correlation in October and December, confirming a small set of outliers distorted national patterns; November showed strong correlation even without exclusions.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; ref [15].

insights.insight: Single‑day events drove mass casualties: Oct 1 in Melit saw four clashes each >100 deaths (one at 163); Oct 22 in Tamboul (Sharg Al Jazirah) had a 520‑death battle, the year’s deadliest; December included a 280‑death territory‑overtake in Um Algura.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; refs [16][17].

insights.insight: Repeated high‑casualty battles around Al Fasher in late 2024, including several December government‑regain‑territory events each with 50–89 deaths, made the siege a sustained mass‑casualty setting.
insights.context: From Khartoum Frontlines to Deadly Clusters; ref [17].

insights.insight: RSF’s footprint expanded dramatically in 2024, appearing in more districts and locations than the army; in October alone RSF reached 78 admin2s and 320 locations—about double the army’s footprint.
insights.context: Occupation, Predation; ref [18].

insights.insight: RSF expanded its presence from 371 locations in 2023 to 1,032 in 2024, nearly tripling geographic spread—an unmatched surge among actors.
insights.context: Occupation, Predation; ref [19].

insights.insight: RSF and allied political militias dominated civilian targeting in 2024, responsible for roughly 1,200 of 1,522 recorded attacks on civilians, concentrated in Al Jazirah (Al Hasahisa, Wad Medani) and North Darfur (Kutum, El Fasher).

insights.insight: Civilian‑targeting incidents were often low‑fatality or with no confirmed deaths, forming a long tail of predatory coercion (beatings, raids, roadside assaults) that shaped daily life under occupation.

insights.insight: Looting/property destruction (430+ events) and abductions (239) outnumbered pitched clashes and were widely dispersed, densest in Al Jazirah, Khartoum, and Darfur—signaling sustained coercive control.
